## Goals

At the end of this Lab session, we should:

- know the types and structures of spatial data in `raster` form and be able to work with them\
- understand the basics of modern spatial packages in R\



## {{< iconify noto-v1 package >}} Setting up R Packages



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Plotting Maps
library(tidyverse) # Maps using ggplot() + geom_sf()
library(ggformula) # Maps using gf_sf()
# For Spatial Data Frame Processing
library(sf)
library(sfheaders) # Handcrafted Map data
library(terra)
library(tidyterra) # tidy syntax for terra operations + plotting
library(stars)
# Downloading Raster Data
library(neonUtilities)
```

## {{< iconify openmoji japanese-symbol-for-beginner >}} Introduction

We will get used to the idea of `raster` data, which is the second important data format in Geospatial Information Systems(GIS).

## What is Raster Data?

Raster Data is should remind you of the TV screen, where a light beam scans lines across the screen from L to R, progressively going downward with each line. At each pixel location on the screen, the beam either intensifies or de-intensifies, or adds a shade of colour, and so on.

So imagine a grid of values where each cell contains a number. Raster or "gridded" data are data that are saved in pixels. In the spatial world, each pixel represents an area on the Earth's surface. For example in the raster below, each pixel represents a particular land cover class that would be found in that location in the real world.

![Raster Data from National Ecological Science Network(NEON), <https://neonscience.org>](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEONScience/NEON-Data-Skills/main/graphics/raster-general/raster_concept.png){#fig-raster-data}


Raster data has three principal attributes:

- `extent`: think of the `boundingbox` we used with vector data
- `resolution`: a measure of the area covered by each cell in the data
- `CRS`: the projection of the data

## What does Raster Data look like in R?



## Raster Data Processing Packages

The most important and modern package is `{{terra}}`. However, `{{terra}}` does not support the `tidyverse` idiom, so we will use `{{tidyterra}}` which combines the features of `{{terra}}` and also adds a few useful functions".

- `{{tidyterra}}` can manipulate the following classes of terra objects:
    - `SpatVector` objects, which represent vector data such as points, lines, or polygon geometries.
    - `SpatRaster` objects, which represent raster data in the form of a grid consisting of equally sized rectangles. Each rectangle can contain one or more values.
    - Furthermore, `{{tidyterra}}` extends the functionality of the ggplot2 package (Wickham 2016) by providing additional geoms and stats like `geom_spatraster()` and `geom_spatvector()`, as well as carefully chosen *scales and color palettes* specifically designed for map production.

We will also use the package `{{neonUtilities}}` to download raster data from the web, in much the same was as we used `{{osmplotr}}` with vector data. 

## Our First Raster Map in R


Let us download some vegetation data from the [Neon Data website](https://neonscience.org/data):

```{{r}}
#| label: download-raster
#| message: false
#| cache: true

# Downloading a Land Cover Raster from NEON
# https://www.neonscience.org/data-products/DP1.00016.001
# This is a Land Cover Classification product
# Download the data
neonUtilities::byTileAOP(dpID='DP3.30024.001', # lidar elevation
          site='HARV',
          year='2022',
          easting=732000,
          northing=4713500,
          check.size=FALSE, # set to TRUE or remove if you want to check the size before downloading
          savepath = "data/neon-raster/", progress = FALSE)

```

We will run the chunck above in our Console, **one time**, so as not to flood the NEON server with queries. Now we can read the raster data into R using `terra::rast()` function:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
# Read the raster data
harv <- terra::rast("data/neon-raster/DP3.30024.001/neon-aop-products/2022/FullSite/D01/2022_HARV_7/L3/DiscreteLidar/DSMGtif/NEON_D01_HARV_DP3_732000_4713000_DSM.tif")

str(harv)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
S4 class 'SpatRaster' [package "terra"]
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
tidyterra::glimpse(harv)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#  A SpatRaster 1,000 x 1,000 x 1 layer (1e+06 cells)
#  Resolution (x / y): (1 / 1)
#  Projected CRS: WGS 84 / UTM zone 18N
#  CRS projection units: meter <m>
#  Extent (x / y) : ([  732,000 /   733,000] , [4,713,000 / 4,714,000])

$ NEON_D01_HARV_DP3_732000_4713000_DSM <dbl> 412.66, 410.95, 412.24, 412.80, 4…
```


:::
:::


We have one `layer` in our data. It has a million cells, and rhe resolution is `1 meter X 1 meter`. Let us plot this using the `{{ggplot}}` geometry functions *within* `{{tidyterra}}`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
ggplot() + tidyterra::geom_spatraster(data = harv) + scale_fill_whitebox_c(palette = "muted",
    n.breaks = 12, guide = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) + labs(fill = "", title = "Vegetation at the Harvard Forest Site",
    subtitle = "") + theme_custom()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in `theme_custom()`:
! could not find function "theme_custom"
```


:::
:::


Let us try one more map, this time with contour lines. Here we use an internal file that is part of the `{{tidyterra}}`package:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Contour lines for a specific layer

f_volcano <- system.file("extdata/volcano2.tif", package = "tidyterra")
volcano2 <- terra::rast(f_volcano)

ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = volcano2) + geom_spatraster_contour(data = volcano2,
    breaks = seq(80, 200, 5)) + scale_fill_whitebox_c() + coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
    labs(fill = "elevation")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error:
! OGRCreateCoordinateTransformation(): transformation not available
```


:::
:::


Both these maps should give us a flavour of what is possible with the `{{tidyterra}}`package.
